title: Four senses
hook: medieval readers found four layers: literal, allegorical, moral, and where it leads

segments.voice: Yesterday, inspiration: scripture as God-breathed, like dust coming alive in Genesis. Your line was god-breathed. Did a deep breath bring the picture back? Day one thousand sixty-seven.

How many meanings can one word hold? Try Jerusalem. To a pilgrim, it's a city on a hill, with walls and a temple. To a monk named John Cassian, writing for other monks, it could be four things at once: the earthly city, the church, the human soul, and the city of God waiting at the end of everything. One word, four rooms. For many medieval readers, that wasn't a trick. It was how you read the Bible carefully. Today's word: four senses.
screen: `A CITY, A CHURCH, A SOUL, HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: The four senses are four layers of meaning in a passage of scripture. First, the literal: what the words say and what happened. Second, the allegorical: what the passage shows about Christ and the church. Third, the moral: what it asks of you, how to live. Fourth, the one with the hardest name, the anagogical: where it leads, toward the end of all things and the life to come. A little Latin rhyme, tradition says, summed it up. In plain English it runs something like: the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral what to do, and the anagogy where you're going. And there's a seed of it in the Bible itself. In Galatians, Paul tells the story of Abraham's two sons, one by Hagar the bondmaid and one by the freewoman, and then says: "Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants." A story about a family, read as a story about God's promises. The medieval teachers also kept a rule. Thomas Aquinas taught that the other senses stand on the literal one: you don't float off to heaven until you know what the text actually says. Churches have kept this differently. Catholic teaching still names the four senses. Orthodox readers draw deeply on the early fathers' spiritual readings. Reformers such as Luther and Calvin pushed hard for the plain sense, wary of allegories that could make a verse mean anything, while still reading Christ throughout the scriptures. All of them were asking the same thing: how deep does this go?

Here's the practice: read one story in all four ways. Take a short one. A shepherd counts his sheep and finds one missing, so he goes after it, and carries it home on his shoulders, glad. Settle, and breathe. First, literal: see the hillside, the search, the sheep on his shoulders. Then allegorical: some readers have seen the shepherd as Christ, seeking. Then moral: who has gone missing from your circle, and will you go looking? Then where it leads: Jesus ends the story with joy in heaven. Move through slowly, one layer per breath or two. If you pray, stay in whichever layer feels like prayer. The bell holds the time.
Four senses. Literal, allegorical, moral, and where it leads: the medieval way of reading one passage on four floors at once.
Your line: layers of meaning. Today, when a sentence catches you, a lyric, a sign, a line in a book, ask what it says, and then what else it might say. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching names the literal sense and three spiritual senses of scripture; Orthodox preaching often draws on the early fathers' spiritual readings, and Protestant preaching, following the Reformers, stresses the plain sense of the text.

fork.setup: you're a student in a medieval school, reading the word Jerusalem in a psalm. your teacher asks for the fourth sense: where does it lead?
options: the city in Judea, with walls and a temple.
the human soul, and how to live.
the city of God at the end of all things.
fork.reveal: the fourth sense points to the end: the city of God. the city with walls is the literal sense, and the soul is the moral one.

original.note: Greek: usually explained as a leading up; the name of the fourth sense, where a text leads.

notes: The Jerusalem example (city, church, soul, heavenly city) follows John Cassian, Conferences 14.8; confirm the attribution and that 'writing for other monks' is fair.

The Latin rhyme (Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria, moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia) is paraphrased, not quoted, and not attributed (usually credited to Augustine of Dacia). 'Carried around the medieval schools' – confirm.

Aquinas, Summa I.1.10: the spiritual senses are founded on the literal. Catholic teaching names the four senses (Catechism 115–118). Reformers (Luther, Calvin) described as pressing for the plain sense while reading Christ throughout scripture. Check fairness to each.
Practice: 'some readers have seen the shepherd as Christ' (Luke 15:3–7); confirm.
Original: ἀναγωγή as 'a leading up' is an etymology, attributed ('usually explained'). Confirm.
